story.headline: Council of States backs 90% UBS capital rule
story.summary: The Ständerat voted that UBS must back foreign subsidiaries with 90% Common Equity Tier 1, siding with Keller-Sutter over its own committee's 50/50 compromise.
story.display_body: The Council of States voted on Wednesday 23 September to require UBS to back its foreign subsidiaries with 90% Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1 — the highest-quality, loss-absorbing "hard" capital), rejecting a softer compromise from its own committee. The chamber (Ständerat — the cantonal chamber of parliament) discarded a 50/50 formula floated by its Economic Affairs Committee, under which UBS could have met half the requirement with cheaper AT1 bonds (Additional Tier 1 — debt that converts to equity or is written down in a crisis). Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter had argued the 50/50 version was legally shaky because AT1 instruments are not aligned with international regulatory standards, and financial-market regulator FINMA and the Swiss National Bank both back the Federal Council's tougher line as sensible and bearable for the bank. UBS itself puts the recurring cost of the stricter capital rules at close to 3 billion francs a year, and CEO Sergio Ermotti has argued they would undercut the bank's international competitiveness; the size of that price is disputed among economists. The 90% decision is a first reading and still has to clear the National Council and reconciliation.
story.why: This is the core fight of Switzerland's post–Credit Suisse "too-big-to-fail" overhaul — how much of a buffer the country's only remaining global bank must hold so taxpayers aren't again on the hook for a rescue, weighed against the cost to a bank whose balance sheet dwarfs the Swiss economy.

story.headline: Report: fixed F-35 price never existed
story.summary: A National Council oversight committee concluded the guaranteed fixed price for 36 F-35 jets never existed and that the defence department misled parliament and the public.
story.display_body: A parliamentary oversight report concludes that the "fixed price" Switzerland was promised for its 36 F-35 fighter jets never existed, and that the defence department misled parliament and the public about it for years. The National Council's Control Committee (CdG-N — the oversight body that scrutinises the federal administration) published its findings on 8 September after more than a year of work, and Le Temps laid out the detail on Wednesday 23 September. From November 2021 the defence department (DDPS) — under then-minister Viola Amherd until her resignation in March 2025, then her successor Martin Pfister — insisted on a guaranteed fixed price of about 6 billion francs; only on 13 August 2025 did Pfister concede Switzerland "cannot impose a fixed price," after costs had risen by roughly a billion. The committee found that at every point the available information showed there was no agreement on a lump-sum fixed price, and dismissed as baseless the argument that Washington had contractually agreed one. Responsibilities for the misleading communication remain to be assigned.
story.why: the F-35 buy is Switzerland's largest-ever arms procurement and was sold to voters on a cost promise the state's own oversight body now says was never real — a credibility problem for the defence department heading into further budget fights. Le Temps, 23.09.2026 [paywalled — read via the free 20-second summary]

story.headline: Parmelin defends multilateralism at UN
story.summary: Swiss President Guy Parmelin used his UN General Assembly address to defend multilateralism and the UN, warning against a world where might comes before right.
story.display_body: Swiss President Guy Parmelin used his address to the UN General Assembly to make an unusually pointed defence of multilateralism, warning against a world where "might comes before right.". Opening with an image of Switzerland as a land of mountains, valleys and languages that learned to build "passes, bridges and tunnels" over what divides, Parmelin argued that in such a world small states like Switzerland are disadvantaged and depend on international law and the UN. Speaking to SRF after listening to US President Donald Trump's Tuesday address — which he called unsurprising — he said the UN is "weakened" but "indispensable," and called for closer cooperation among small and mid-sized countries to push the pendulum back. For a Federal Councillor from the SVP (Swiss People's Party — the eurosceptic right that has often been cool on the UN), the endorsement was notably emphatic. SRF, 23.09.2026

story.headline: US and Iran hold mediated Hormuz talks
story.summary: The US and Iran held hours of indirect, mediator-shuttled UNGA talks on ending their war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, though their accounts of the meeting differed.
story.display_body: The United States and Iran held hours of indirect, mediator-shuttled talks on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Tuesday 22 September, aimed at ending their war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz — though the two sides' accounts differed sharply. US special envoy Steve Witkoff said mediators "shuttled between" the American and Iranian delegations throughout the day and completed a round of discussions he hoped would prove "constructive"; Trump went further, describing a three-hour meeting involving Witkoff and Jared Kushner with "a lot of momentum" toward an agreement, before the White House clarified he had not himself attended. Iranian state media confirmed a meeting between Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Witkoff, saying it came at Washington's insistence and that Tehran's conditions for reopening the strait include lifting the US naval blockade, releasing frozen Iranian assets and ending the war. The talks come against a backdrop of resumed strikes and escalating rhetoric — Trump used his General Assembly speech to threaten to "annihilate" Iran.
story.why: The Strait of Hormuz carries a large share of the world's seaborne oil, so any blockade or its lifting moves energy prices globally; the gap between the US and Iranian read-outs is a reminder to treat "momentum" claims cautiously.

story.headline: France, UK, Canada press Palestinian statehood
story.summary: At a UNGA meeting Guterres warned the two-state solution risks collapse as France, the UK and Canada pressed for Palestinian sovereignty.
story.display_body: France, the United Kingdom and Canada pressed for Palestinian statehood at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday 22 September, as Secretary-General António Guterres warned the two-state solution risks collapse. At a high-level meeting co-hosted by Canada, France, Saudi Arabia and the UK, Guterres said the conditions for a "viable and sovereign Palestinian State are being systematically erased" by Israeli settlement expansion and West Bank settler violence. French President Emmanuel Macron — noting France was among about a dozen states that recognised Palestine a year ago — called the world's failure to act on aid restrictions to Gaza "shameful" and asked what credibility inaction leaves. Trump had hours earlier hailed his own Gaza plan from the same rostrum; the White House dismissed Macron's criticism. The meeting built on the 2025 New York Declaration and the Security Council–endorsed October 2025 ceasefire, which Gaza authorities say has continued to see Palestinian deaths.
story.why: It marks a widening split between Washington and key Western allies over how to end the Gaza war and whether recognition of a Palestinian state can be turned into anything concrete on the ground.

story.headline: Trump signs Greenland military-bases deal
story.summary: Trump signed a security accord with Denmark and Greenland formalising two US military bases on the island, converting last week's framework into a signed deal.
story.display_body: Trump signed a security agreement with Denmark and Greenland on Tuesday 22 September, formalising two US military bases on the island after months of pressure to "own" it. The deal — signed on the UN sidelines with Greenlandic Premier Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Danish PM Mette Frederiksen, and released in full by the White House — provides for the US to re-establish a base at Narsarsuaq in the south and set up another at Mestersvig on the east coast. Trump called it "tremendous" for Europe and the US; it converts the framework announced a week earlier into a signed accord rather than adding new territory.
story.why: It defuses, for now, a NATO-straining dispute between two allies and cements a much larger US military footprint in the strategically pivotal, resource-rich Arctic — while leaving open how far Washington's territorial ambitions toward Greenland go.

story.headline: Zelenskyy offers Russia an energy ceasefire
story.summary: After meeting Trump in New York, Zelenskyy said Ukraine is ready for a mutual energy ceasefire with Russia and warned of a planned Russian attack.
story.display_body: Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday 22 September that Kyiv is ready for a mutual "energy ceasefire" with Russia, after meeting Trump for about 40 minutes in New York. Zelenskyy said Kyiv would halt strikes on Russian energy facilities if Moscow stops targeting Ukraine's power, heating and water systems — but stressed there was no discussion of Ukraine unilaterally ending attacks on Russia's oil industry, and warned on Telegram that Russia is planning "a new massive attack." He described the Trump talks, which focused on ending the invasion "before winter," as "positive and productive." Trump — facing record-low approval and high petrol prices before November's US midterm elections — has voiced concern that Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries are pushing up global diesel prices.
story.why: an energy truce would spare civilians a fifth winter of blackouts and could ease world fuel prices, but the framing exposes competing pressures — Kyiv's leverage over Russian refining versus Washington's worry about pump prices. Al Jazeera, 23.09.2026

story.headline: EU delists Usmanov and Fridman from sanctions
story.summary: The EU extended Russia sanctions for 36 months but removed oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, a carve-out Kyiv called shameful.
story.display_body: The EU agreed on Tuesday 22 September to extend its Russia sanctions for a further 36 months but removed two oligarchs, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, from the list — a carve-out Kyiv called "shameful.". Facing a Wednesday deadline and the need for unanimity, member states rolled the regime over until September 2029 for roughly 3,000 individuals and entities, replacing the usual six-month renewals; France and Luxembourg drove the exemptions for the two men, both seen as close to the Kremlin. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Moscow was "celebrating" the delistings as a sign of impunity and European division.
story.why: the longer rollover shields the sanctions from repeated veto fights, but delisting high-profile oligarchs to buy that stability hands Moscow a symbolic win and tests the credibility of the EU's pressure campaign. DW, 22.09.2026

story.headline: Kiir dissolves South Sudan government
story.summary: President Salva Kiir dissolved South Sudan's transitional unity government and named a caretaker administration ahead of first national elections set for 22 December.
story.display_body: South Sudan's President Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional unity government on Tuesday 22 September and appointed a caretaker administration ahead of the country's first-ever national elections, set for 22 December. A decree read on state media removed all vice-presidents, ministers and local administrators and dissolved the national and state assemblies, while keeping the judiciary and security bodies and leaving Kiir in office through the election period. It followed parliament's approval of changes to the elections law that let him stay in power and allow a vote to proceed without a permanent constitution or census.
story.why: the move unwinds the power-sharing arrangement from the 2018 deal that ended South Sudan's civil war, and critics warn it concentrates unchecked power in Kiir's hands just as the fragile state heads to a long-delayed vote. Al Jazeera, 23.09.2026

story.headline: Belgium and Rwanda restore diplomatic ties
story.summary: Belgium and Rwanda restored relations 18 months after a rupture over the DRC conflict, crediting Qatari mediation.
story.display_body: Belgium and Rwanda restored diplomatic relations on Tuesday 22 September, 18 months after expelling each other's diplomats over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, crediting Qatari mediation. In a joint statement, the two governments thanked Qatar for facilitating their first talks in June 2025; Doha, which has also mediated between the DRC, Rwanda and the M23 armed group (a Rwanda-backed insurgency in eastern Congo), said it would keep pushing diplomacy across Africa's Great Lakes region and the Gulf.
story.why: a rare de-escalation around one of Africa's deadliest ongoing conflicts, and a marker of Qatar's growing role as a go-between in disputes far from its usual Middle East remit. Al Jazeera, 23.09.2026

story.headline: Antiprotons take their first road trip from CERN
story.summary: The BASE collaboration transported 92 trapped antiprotons out of CERN's Antimatter Factory by road, a first for antimatter.
story.display_body: Until now, every precision comparison of matter and antimatter has had to be carried out inside CERN's Antimatter Factory in Geneva, where magnetic-field jitter from the accelerator complex limits how sharply physicists can measure an antiproton's properties. The BASE collaboration built BASE-STEP — a cryogenic, self-contained Penning trap (a device that holds charged particles with electric and magnetic fields in ultrahigh vacuum) engineered to be transportable — and used it to carry 92 trapped antiprotons out of the facility by road, the first time antimatter has ever been moved by truck. The antiprotons survived the journey, showing that the particles can in principle be relocated to quieter "offline" laboratories away from the accelerator hall.
story.why: Measuring antiprotons in a low-noise lab could sharpen tests of whether matter and antimatter obey exactly the same laws (CPT symmetry) by up to 100-fold — any discrepancy would be a clue to why the universe is made of matter at all.

story.headline: Steady laser drives thorium-229 nuclear clock
story.summary: A continuous-wave laser excited the thorium-229 nuclear transition in absorption, enabling faster readout for a solid-state nuclear clock.
story.display_body: Most atomic clocks tick on transitions in an atom's electron cloud; the thorium-229 nucleus is unusual in having an energy jump low enough to be driven by laser light, which would make a "nuclear clock" far less sensitive to stray fields and potentially more stable. Earlier demonstrations excited that transition with pulsed 148-nanometre ultraviolet lasers, but only a tiny fraction of the photons ever landed on the narrow resonance. Here the team excited the nucleus inside a calcium-fluoride crystal using a continuous-wave (steady, narrow-bandwidth) solid-state laser at sub-nanowatt power and — crucially — detected the resonance in absorption rather than by waiting for the nucleus to re-emit light, which removes the slow fluorescence step that had bottlenecked readout and allows much faster clock cycles. They also found one thorium site sitting in an unusually quiet electric environment (a static crystal-field gradient below 0.1 V/Å², versus roughly 100 V/Å² seen before).
story.why: Faster, cleaner interrogation is a concrete engineering step toward a robust solid-state nuclear clock — a device that could test whether the "constants" of nature actually drift over time.

story.headline: Quantum simulator watches a force string snap
story.summary: A trapped-ion quantum simulator resolved string-breaking dynamics in a Z2 lattice gauge theory, a table-top model of quark confinement.
story.display_body: The strong nuclear force behaves like an elastic string: pull two quarks apart and the energy stored between them keeps rising until the string "breaks," spawning fresh particle pairs — which is why isolated quarks are never seen. Simulating that process from first principles overwhelms classical computers, so a Duke-led group emulated it on a programmable trapped-ion quantum simulator (individual trapped ions standing in for the quantum field), using focused laser beams to set site-by-site effective magnetic fields that encode a simplified (1+1-dimensional) Z₂ lattice gauge theory — a stripped-down toy model of confinement. With spatial and temporal resolution they watched isolated charges spread freely when the string tension was switched off, and stay confined — the string breaking into new pairs — when it was on.
story.why: It is a clean, controllable table-top window onto confinement, one of the least computable features of the theory that governs protons and neutrons.

story.headline: Epigenetic silencer shuts off hepatitis B in animals
story.summary: The epigenetic silencer CRMA-1001 methylated and durably repressed hepatitis B virus DNA in mice and non-human primates.
story.display_body: Chronic hepatitis B is hard to cure because the virus leaves behind both free-floating (episomal) and genome-integrated DNA that today's drugs suppress but rarely silence for good. CRMA-1001 is an epigenetic silencer — a designed protein that does not cut DNA but instead deposits methyl chemical tags to switch off transcription — aimed at both forms of hepatitis B virus (HBV) DNA. In mouse models a single dose cut viral biomarkers more than 1,000-fold (a >3-log₁₀ reduction), and three doses left up to 90% of animals with undetectable surface antigen and HBV DNA six months later; in non-human primates the main effect was a transient rise in liver enzymes at the highest dose, with no detectable off-target silencing across the human genome.
story.why: This is a preclinical proof of concept — not yet a human therapy — for a "functional cure" that turns the virus off rather than merely holding it down, and the animal data are meant to support taking CRMA-1001 into clinical trials.

story.headline: Simulations grow JWST's overmassive black holes
story.summary: Cosmological simulations naturally form million-solar-mass black-hole seeds that reproduce JWST's overmassive little red dots.
story.display_body: JWST has turned up a puzzling population of "little red dots" — compact red galaxies in the first billion years of cosmic time whose central black holes look far too massive for their host galaxies compared with the nearby universe. Using fully cosmological radiation-hydrodynamics simulations (which follow gas, radiation and gravity together), the authors find that heavy black-hole "seeds" of about a million solar masses form naturally in dense protocluster regions — roughly ten times heavier than standard theory expects. Those seeds develop dense, optically thick disks whose electron scattering broadens their hydrogen emission lines to mimic the little-red-dot signature, then accrete above the usual Eddington limit (the point where radiation pressure normally chokes off infall) to reach about 3×10⁷ solar masses by redshift z≈8.
story.why: It offers a single self-consistent origin story for objects that had strained existing models, suggesting the early universe forged supermassive-black-hole seeds far more readily than thought.

story.headline: Einstein Probe finds a new Galactic magnetar
story.summary: Einstein Probe discovered the magnetar EP J223759.5+531421, with IXPE confirming ~7% X-ray polarization from two surface hot spots.
story.display_body: On 28 June 2026 the Einstein Probe X-ray satellite caught a new magnetar — a neutron star with an extreme magnetic field — flaring in our Galaxy, now catalogued EP J223759.5+531421. Follow-up with Einstein Probe, XMM-Newton, NuSTAR, SVOM and IXPE found 6-second X-ray pulsations and a spin-down rate implying a dipole magnetic field around 2.6×10¹⁴ gauss (hundreds of trillions of times Earth's) and a characteristic age near 34,000 years; over the first month its X-ray luminosity faded by roughly half. A companion study from IXPE [arXiv:2609.25958], the first satellite that measures the polarization (the alignment) of X-rays, adds that the emission is about 7% polarized, consistent with two hot regions (near 0.5 and 1 keV) on the star's surface.
story.why: Magnetars are the strongest magnets known, and catching one this early in an outburst with both precise timing and polarization lets astronomers test how their crusts and magnetospheres actually behave.

story.headline: First retrograde planet found around an M dwarf
story.summary: Geneva's NIRPS spectrograph showed the sub-Neptune GJ 3090 b on a retrograde orbit, the first such misalignment measured around an M dwarf.
story.display_body: The angle between a star's spin and a planet's orbit is a fossil record of how the planet migrated inward. Using the Geneva-led NIRPS spectrograph (a near-infrared instrument on the European Southern Observatory's 3.6-metre telescope in Chile) together with HARPS, the team measured the Rossiter–McLaughlin effect — the subtle spectral distortion a transiting planet imprints as it blocks part of the rotating stellar disk — for the sub-Neptune GJ 3090 b. They find the planet on a retrograde orbit (circling opposite to its star's spin), the first such misaligned orbit measured around an M dwarf, the small, cool, abundant stars that host most of the galaxy's planets.
story.why: A backwards orbit points to a violent dynamical past rather than gentle disk migration, and it pushes these spin–orbit measurements into the M-dwarf systems where most rocky planets — and most searches for habitable worlds — are found.
